newsitem.title: UK: Oil holds $18 and waits for US drivers to rev up.
newsitem.headline: Oil holds $18 and waits for US drivers to rev up.

text.p: Rocky oil prices appear to have found a floor around $18 a barrel for benchmark Brent blend in anticipation of a rise in demand for gasoline from U.S. motorists ahead of the key driving season in the United States, traders and analysts said.
Concern over Iran's diplomatic standoff with the European Union also has helped staunch the 30 percent three-month slide in crude values.

"Fundamentals still don't look that great but they aren't the only thing that determine prices," said Scott Carter, senior trader at Tosco Petroleum Corp in London. "As long as the funds don't buy we might settle into a range between $17 and the high $18s."
"Another big move down in the next few weeks is unlikely," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division at Bankers Trust International in London.
London Brent crude has slumped $7 a barrel from just below $25 in early January, hitting a nine-month low at $17.65. Brent futures for May were trading at $18.05-$18.10 on Monday morning.

Many dealers believe this year's slide was exacerbated by speculative financial funds baling out of oil and commodities after big gains in 1996 and fears of a a false start in the global economic recovery.
Funds may have helped tip oil markets over the edge but weak fundamentals -- mild winter weather and a wave of new crude supplies -- did the real damage to prices, say traders.
Some believe there is a small chance of funds coming back in to buy in the coming weeks, particularly if stock markets around the world stay weak.
"We still feel pretty comfortable with our full year forecast of $20 a barrel which is predicated on the second quarter averaging $18," said oil specialist Rick Jones at NatWest Securities in London.
NatWest sees Brent rising a dollar a barrel in subsequent quarters to $19 and $20.
The downdraft from the price fall has even been enough to rattle countries of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) who now face renewed pressure on national budgets.
Many had raised their price forecasts for this year after big prices gains in 1996 had produced unexpected windfalls.
But any action from OPEC is highly unlikely. The last time the group cut output to prop up oil prices was more than 10 years ago.
Instead, demand for refined oil products seems to be the key to halting the slide.
The growing price gap between refined oil products and crude oil has left some dealers puzzled. Typically, weak oil markets leave a narrow gap and poor profit margins at refineries.
The gap has recently been forced open by strong Asian demand for gasoline and diesel which in turn has meant big profit margins for refiners this year.
"The key to this market has been a combination of strong products in Asia and cheap crude in Europe. The further east you go the better the demand is," said a London-based trader.
Many dealers had expected Asian demand to halt the precipitous slide in Brent prices in March.
There was a $2 a barrel corrective rally last month but weak fundamentals punched the market back down.
With Asian demand beginning to show some signs of flattening out, dealers are shifting their gaze to the United States where gasoline demand is expected to kick-in ahead of the summer driving season.
Demand is expected to rise 1.8 percent to 8.14 million barrels per day (bpd) this summer, according to the Energy Information Administration (EIA).
To meet demand growth "much hinges on the ability of U.S. refiners to step up gasoline production levels to new highs, and on the continued availability of foreign supplies," the EIA said recently.
The United States sucked in huge imports from Europe in December and January but it has been less thirsty since then.
Second quarter imports picked up last year to 374,000 bpd from 308,000 bpd in 1995 and gasoline stocks in the United States are low.

There has been a four-year downward trend in gasoline stocks which now stand nearly three percent below year-ago levels. In Europe, gasoline stocks are just over three percent down on year-ago levels.
A trader said Asian demand in general and U.S. demand for gasoline were the key pillars supporting the market and "one of these two would have to falter" for the market to fall lower.
